title: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
summary: Exact unlearning with SISA, why gradient ascent collapses and how NPO fixes it, replacement methods (WHP, RMU), how TOFU and MUSE measure forgetting, and why relearning and quantization undo it.
outcomes: Explain what exact unlearning guarantees and compute how SISA's sharding and slicing cut retraining cost
Explain why gradient ascent collapses and how NPO's adaptive weight slows divergence
Describe how Who's Harry Potter and RMU replace knowledge instead of pushing it down
Compute a TOFU truth ratio and read forget quality, utility and MUSE privacy leakage against a retrained model
Explain why fine-tuning, probing and 4-bit quantization can recover approximately unlearned knowledge

lessons.title: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA

blocks.md:
A trained model is a compressed summary of its training data, and large models can memorize parts of it verbatim. So deleting a row from the database does not delete its influence: the weights still carry it. Three pressures make this matter: privacy law (the GDPR right to erasure that motivated Bourtoule et al.), copyrighted text that should not have been trained on, and hazardous knowledge (for example, bioweapon details) that a lab wants out of a released model.

**Machine unlearning** is the task of removing the influence of a chosen **forget set** of training data (or of a body of knowledge) from an already trained model, while keeping everything else the model can do.

The gold standard is simple to state. Let $D$ be the training set and $D_f \subset D$ the forget set. **Exact unlearning** produces a model that could have come from training on $D \setminus D_f$ from the start. Retraining from scratch on the remaining data achieves this by definition, and it is the reference every other method is measured against.

The problem is cost. Llama-2-7B took over 184K GPU-hours to pretrain (as reported by Eldan and Russinovich), and deletion requests arrive one at a time. Nobody retrains a 7B model per request.

**SISA training** (Bourtoule et al., 2019) keeps the guarantee of exact unlearning but makes retraining cheaper by limiting how far any one point can spread. It changes how you train *before* any deletion happens:

1. **Sharded**: split $D$ into $S$ disjoint shards.
2. **Isolated**: train a separate model on each shard.
3. **Sliced**: inside a shard, add data in $R$ slices and checkpoint before each one.
4. **Aggregated**: combine the shard models at inference, for example by majority vote.

scenes.caption: Sharded: split the training set into S disjoint shards (here S = 4). Every point lives in exactly one shard.
Isolated: train one constituent model per shard, with no information shared between them. A point can only influence the model of its own shard.
Aggregated: at inference every constituent model predicts and the simplest aggregation is a majority vote over labels.
A user asks to delete a point that sits in shard B. Models A, C and D never saw it, so they are already exactly what retraining without it would give.
Only model B is retrained on shard B minus the point. The cost is one shard, about N/S points, instead of all N.

blocks.title: Slicing: resume from the last checkpoint that never saw the point

scenes.caption: A toy SISA layout: N = 16 points, S = 4 shards, R = 4 slices per shard (one point per slice here). Columns are slices in the order they are added to training.
Shard B's model is trained incrementally: slice 1, then slices 1 and 2, and so on. The parameters are saved to disk just before each new slice is added.
Point d6 must be unlearned. It sits in slice 3 of shard B. Every training step from slice 3 onward saw it; the checkpoint saved before slice 3 never did.
Load the checkpoint saved before slice 3 and redo only the later training on the remaining points. Shards A, C, D and the first two slices of B are untouched. The price is storing the checkpoints.

blocks.md: For a single request, sharding means retraining one shard instead of the whole set. Slicing adds more: if the deleted point sits in slice $r$, you resume from the checkpoint saved before slice $r$ and redo only the later training. Under the paper's simplifying assumptions (uniform requests, training time proportional to the number of samples processed, epochs rebalanced so sliced and unsliced training cost the same), the best case, a point in the last slice, gives this speed-up for one request:

blocks.caption: With the paper's main setting S = 20, R = 50 this is 20x from sharding and 510x combined in the best case. Averaged over where the point falls, slicing gains at most 1.5x (the paper's Eq. 4), so about 30x combined; batched requests lower it further.

blocks.md: Requests accumulate. If $K$ requests are batched and each hits a uniformly random shard, the expected fraction of shards that must be retrained is $1 - (1 - 1/S)^K$ (this is the batch-cost formula from the paper divided by $N$, ignoring the $K$ deleted points themselves).

blocks.title: How much of the model a batch of K deletions touches

scenes.caption: With S = 20 shards and uniformly random requests, one request touches 1/20 of the model. 20 requests already touch 64.2% of the shards in expectation.

At K = 3S = 60 requests, 95.4% of shards need retraining, close to retraining everything. This matches the paper's observation that sharding helps while requests stay below about three times the shard count.
Few shards (S = 5) saturate almost immediately. More shards delay saturation but make each constituent model a weaker learner because it sees less data.

blocks.md: Measured results are therefore modest. With 20 shards and 50 slices, SISA was 4.63x faster than retraining from scratch on Purchase (8 requests) and 2.45x on SVHN (18 requests), at under 2 percentage points of accuracy loss. On ImageNet the speed-up was only 1.36x, with a large accuracy drop that transfer learning reduced. The reason is the **weak learner** problem: each shard model sees only $1/S$ of the data, which hurts most on complex tasks.

SISA is a training-time design decision. It cannot be retrofitted onto a model that was already trained on all the data, which is the situation for every existing LLM. That is why the rest of this course is about **approximate** unlearning: editing an existing model so it behaves *as if* it had been retrained, without a guarantee.

Exact unlearning means the result is what retraining without the forget set would give. SISA keeps that guarantee by confining each point's influence to one shard and one suffix of slices, so only that part is retrained.

blocks.question: A SISA system with S = 20 shards batches 60 uniformly random deletion requests before retraining. Roughly what fraction of the shard models must be retrained?
options: About 95%, almost every shard is hit at least once
About 5%, one shard per batch
About 33%, since 60 / 20 = 3 requests per shard on average
100% exactly, because 60 is larger than 20
blocks.explain: Each shard escapes all 60 requests with probability (1 - 1/20)^60, about 0.046, so about 95.4% of shards are hit at least once. It is not exactly 100% because some shards can get zero requests by chance. This saturation is why SISA's measured speed-ups shrink as requests pile up.

blocks.question: What does slicing cost in exchange for faster unlearning?
options: Lower accuracy, because each slice model is a weaker learner
Storage, because parameters must be checkpointed before every slice
Privacy, because checkpoints leak the deleted point
Nothing, slicing is free
blocks.explain: Slicing changes when data is added inside a shard, not how much data a model sees, so the paper reports no accuracy cost. The overhead is storing the parameter state before each slice is introduced so that retraining can resume from the last checkpoint that never saw the point. Old checkpoints that contain the point must be discarded after unlearning.

lessons.title: Approximate unlearning: gradient ascent, collapse and NPO

blocks.md: **Gradient ascent (GA)** maximizes the usual next-token loss on the forget set, which is the same as minimizing the log-likelihood the model assigns to forget text. Recall from pretraining that the loss is $-\log p_\theta(y \mid x)$ summed over tokens; GA simply flips its sign:

Why does this go wrong? Look at a single token with softmax output $p$ over the vocabulary and correct token $y$. The gradient of $\log p_y$ with respect to the logit $z_y$ is $1 - p_y$. As unlearning succeeds, $p_y$ goes to 0 and the push goes to 1, its maximum. Nothing in the loss says "this one is forgotten, stop", because $\log p_y$ has no lower bound: it heads to minus infinity.

blocks.caption: The push on an already-forgotten example never fades, so weights drift without limit (Zhang et al. show the drift can be linear in the number of steps).

blocks.prompt: Predict: you run gradient ascent with a retain loss for 400 steps on a tiny classifier. The forget answer is gone by step 25. What happens to the weights between step 25 and step 400?
blocks.reveal: They keep moving, roughly linearly. In the toy run below the distance from the starting weights goes from 8.3 at step 25 to 356.9 at step 400, and the displaced probability eventually damages a retain example even though a retain loss is present. In a real LLM every weight is shared by all knowledge, so this drift is what **catastrophic collapse** looks like: utility falls to zero and outputs become gibberish.

blocks.title: Toy run: gradient ascent vs NPO, both with a retain loss

scenes.caption: Simplified model: a 4-class softmax classifier on 3 features, trained on one forget example and two retain examples that share features with it. All start at p = 0.959. Each run then takes 400 steps of its unlearning loss plus a retain loss.
Gradient ascent (GA) on the forget example, plus the normal loss on the retain examples. By step 25 the forget answer is gone (p = 0.000) and the retain examples are fine.

But GA never stops. The weight drift (L2 distance from the starting weights) keeps growing roughly linearly, to 356.9 by step 400. Around step 120 the displaced mass lands on a retain class and one retain example drops to 0.75 despite the retain loss.

NPO with the same retain loss: the forget answer falls to 0.058 by step 25 and 0.001 by step 400, while its weight drift levels off (3.5 at step 25, 6.4 at step 400). Its retain examples end at 0.998.

blocks.md: This matches LLM experiments. On TOFU, Zhang et al. report that standalone gradient ascent makes model utility drop quickly to zero, with forget quality improving only briefly before falling too, and the model ends up generating gibberish (their example answer from GA with a retain loss is "narr narr narr narr"). On the MUSE news benchmark, plain GA scores 0 on both memorization metrics *and* 0 on utility. In practice GA only works with careful early stopping.

Two regularized variants are standard baselines in TOFU:

- **Gradient difference**: ascend on the forget set while descending on the retain set, $\mathcal{L} = -\mathcal{L}(D_f) + \mathcal{L}(D_r)$.
- **KL minimization**: ascend on the forget set while keeping the output distribution on retain data close (in KL divergence) to the original model's.

Both slow the damage but do not remove the cause: the forget term itself is still unbounded.

**Negative Preference Optimization (NPO)** (Zhang, Lin, Bai and Mei, 2024) fixes the cause. Recall that DPO trains on pairs of a preferred and a dispreferred answer, measured against a frozen reference model. NPO keeps only the dispreferred half: every forget example is a negative, and the reference $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is the model before unlearning.

blocks.caption: Bounded below by 0. Its gradient equals the GA gradient multiplied by a per-example weight that shrinks once the example is already unlearned.

blocks.title: Per-example gradient weight: GA vs NPO

scenes.caption: At the start of unlearning the model equals the reference, r = 1 (x = 0), and both methods push with weight 1.
With beta = 1, once an example's probability has fallen to a tenth of the reference (x = -1) NPO's weight is 0.182; at a hundredth it is 0.020. Already-forgotten examples stop pulling the weights.
As beta shrinks toward 0 the NPO curve flattens toward 1, recovering gradient ascent exactly, as the paper proves. Beta is the knob between aggressive and self-limiting.

blocks.md: The paper proves, in a simplified setting, that GA diverges linearly while NPO diverges only logarithmically, which is exponentially slower. Empirically, NPO with a retain loss (NPO+RT) was the only method in their tests to reach forget quality above 0.05 on TOFU's 20% and 30% forget splits, and with tuned loss weights it exceeded 0.05 forget quality with model utility above 0.55 even when forgetting 50% and 90% of TOFU.

"Loss on the forget set went up" is not evidence of good unlearning. GA can drive that loss arbitrarily high by wrecking the model. Always read forget metrics next to utility metrics and next to the retrained reference.

Gradient ascent fails because its objective is unbounded: forgotten examples keep pushing. NPO is gradient ascent with an adaptive weight that fades once an example's probability falls below the reference, so unlearning slows down instead of collapsing.

blocks.question: During NPO with beta = 1, a forget example's probability is now 1% of the reference model's. Compared with plain gradient ascent, how strongly does this example still push the weights?
options: Equally strongly, NPO only changes the loss value, not the gradient
About 2% as strongly, the weight is 2(0.01)/(0.01 + 1) = 0.020
About 50% as strongly, the weight bottoms out at 0.5
Twice as strongly, because NPO doubles the gradient
blocks.explain: NPO's gradient is the GA gradient times W = 2r^b / (r^b + 1). With r = 0.01 and b = 1 that is 0.02 / 1.01, about 0.020. The weight stays near 1 only for very small beta, where NPO behaves like GA; there is no floor at 0.5, it keeps falling toward 0.

blocks.question: A teammate runs gradient ascent on a forget set and reports success because forget-set perplexity rose from 8 to 4,000. What is the most important missing check?
options: Whether the learning rate was warmed up
Utility on retain and general data, compared with a retrained reference
Whether the forget-set perplexity is above 10,000
Whether the model still refuses harmful prompts
blocks.explain: Gradient ascent can raise forget-set loss without limit by damaging the whole model, which is catastrophic collapse. The meaningful question is whether the model now behaves like one never trained on the forget set while keeping its other abilities, so you need retain and general utility and a comparison with the retrained model.

lessons.title: Unlearning by replacement: Who's Harry Potter and RMU

blocks.md: Gradient ascent asks the model to be *wrong* about the forget data. A better target is to be *ignorant*: produce what a model that never read the data would produce. Eldan and Russinovich point out two problems with pushing down the true tokens. In "Harry Potter went up to him and said, Hello. My name is" the next word is Harry, and penalizing it unlearns what "my name is" means. And if "Ron" is pushed down in "Harry Potter's two best friends are", the most likely token simply becomes "Hermione".

**Who's Harry Potter (WHP)** builds *generic predictions*: for every token in the books, an alternative next-token distribution approximating a model that never saw them. It combines two tricks.

1. **Reinforcement bootstrapping**: fine-tune a copy of the model further on the target text, giving a **reinforced model**. Tokens whose logits rise under reinforcement are the story-specific ones, so push them down.
2. **Anchored terms**: replace idiosyncratic names and terms with generic ones (they used GPT-4 to build a dictionary of about 1,500 such pairs), run the baseline model on the translated text, and use its predictions.

blocks.caption: v are logit vectors. The ReLU keeps only logits that the reinforcement increased. The paper uses alpha = 5.

blocks.title: Generic predictions from a reinforced model (toy logits)

scenes.caption: Simplified example, made-up logits: the baseline model completes "Harry Potter went back to class where he saw" with Ron (0.654) or Hermione (0.240).

The reinforced model, fine-tuned further on the books, raises the logits of story-specific tokens (Ron 6.0 to 7.5, Hermione 5.0 to 6.8) while generic tokens barely move. After softmax: 0.653 and 0.324.

Generic logits = baseline minus 5 x ReLU(reinforced minus baseline). Tokens the reinforcement boosted are pushed down hard: the target becomes "the" (0.574), with Ron at 0.004. The model is fine-tuned toward this distribution.

blocks.md: The baseline model is then fine-tuned on the *original* text as input with the generic predictions as target labels. The unlearn set was the books (2.1M tokens) plus 1M tokens of synthetic discussions and wiki-like text, and about 1 GPU-hour of fine-tuning on Llama-2-7b-chat was enough, against the 184K GPU-hours of pretraining.

blocks.title: Who's Harry Potter: familiarity vs benchmarks during fine-tuning

scenes.caption: Step 0, the original Llama-2-7b-chat model. Familiarity is a GPT-4-graded score of how much Harry Potter knowledge completions reveal.
After 20 fine-tuning steps on generic labels, familiarity has fallen from 0.290 to 0.040; benchmarks barely move.
Step 60: familiarity 0.017.
Step 120: familiarity 0.007 while ARC-challenge went 0.440 to 0.414 and BoolQ 0.807 to 0.796. Numbers from the paper's Figure 5. Lesson 5 shows what this metric misses.

blocks.md: The paper's own ablation is telling: reinforcement bootstrapping alone never reduced completion-based familiarity by more than a factor of 0.3. Anchored terms did most of the work, and they need a domain-specific dictionary of replacements (WHP generated it with GPT-4 entity extraction over passages of the books).

**RMU** (Representation Misdirection for Unlearning, Li et al., 2024) targets hazardous knowledge instead of a book series. It was released with **WMDP**, a public benchmark of 3,668 multiple-choice questions (1,273 biosecurity, 1,987 cybersecurity, 408 chemical security) that serve as a proxy for hazardous knowledge, filtered so the questions themselves are not hazardous. RMU changes internal activations rather than output tokens.

blocks.caption: h is the hidden state at layer l, u a fixed random unit vector with entries drawn from [0, 1) then normalized, c a scale (6.5 for Zephyr-7B), alpha the retain weight.

blocks.title: RMU: scramble activations on hazardous text only

nodes.label:
MLPs of layers
l-2, l-1, l (trained)

scenes.caption: RMU edits a model through its hidden states, not its outputs. Only the MLP weights of three consecutive layers ending at layer l are trained (l = 7 for Zephyr-7B).

On forget text, the layer-l activation of every token is pulled toward c times a fixed random unit vector u. Large, meaningless activations early in the network leave later layers unable to use the knowledge.
On retain text, activations are pulled back toward the frozen original model's activations, weighted by alpha (1200 for Zephyr-7B). This keeps general skills.
Each update pairs a forget batch with a retain batch and minimizes forget loss plus alpha times retain loss. To unlearn bio and cyber together, RMU interleaves updates between the two topics.

blocks.title: RMU on Zephyr-7B: WMDP vs MMLU accuracy (%)

scenes.caption: Base Zephyr-7B. WMDP questions are 4-way multiple choice, so 25% is random guessing.
After RMU: WMDP-Bio 31.2% and WMDP-Cyber 28.2%, close to chance, while overall MMLU only moves from 58.1% to 57.1%.
The collateral damage is in neighboring topics: MMLU virology falls from 52.4% to 25.9%, essentially chance. Hazardous and benign knowledge in the same field are hard to separate.

blocks.md: Near-chance accuracy on a multiple-choice proxy shows the model no longer *answers* those questions. It does not show the knowledge is gone from the weights. The WMDP authors say so themselves: because RMU edits only three layers it "perhaps obfuscates knowledge more than unlearns it", and in their appendix fine-tuning on the forget corpus recovered the performance.

Replacement methods give the model something specific to do instead: predict generic tokens (WHP) or produce scrambled activations on hazardous inputs (RMU). That avoids gradient ascent's collapse, but the target behavior is defined only on the inputs you trained on.

blocks.question: In WHP, the baseline model ranks Ron first and Hermione second, but the reinforced model, knowing the books better, ranks Hermione first. Only Hermione's logit rises under reinforcement. What does the generic-prediction formula do?
options: Pushes down both Ron and Hermione equally
Pushes down Hermione but leaves Ron as the top prediction
Leaves both unchanged because the ReLU blocks them
Removes both tokens from the vocabulary
blocks.explain: The formula only subtracts where the reinforced logit exceeds the baseline. Ron's logit did not rise, so it stays and remains the top prediction: the method reinforces a Harry Potter answer instead of removing it. The paper names this exact caveat, which is one reason it adds anchored-term translation.

blocks.question: RMU drops Zephyr-7B's WMDP-Bio accuracy from 63.7% to 31.2% while overall MMLU moves from 58.1% to 57.1%. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The hazardous knowledge has been erased from the weights
RMU has no side effects
The model no longer answers the proxy questions, with little general cost but real loss in nearby topics like virology
WMDP-Bio is now harder than random guessing
blocks.explain: Multiple-choice accuracy near 25% means the model no longer selects the right answers. The table also shows MMLU virology falling from 52.4% to 25.9%, so related benign knowledge was hit. Whether the knowledge is still in the weights is a separate question that fine-tuning attacks answer (Lesson 5).

lessons.title: Measuring forgetting: TOFU, MUSE and the forget-retain tradeoff

blocks.md: Evaluating approximate unlearning is hard for two reasons. First, "does not output it" is weaker than "does not know it". Second, the right target is not zero: a model that never saw the forget set still answers some forget questions from general knowledge, and a model that does *abnormally badly* on the forget set reveals that something was removed there. The yardstick is therefore the **retrained model**, and good unlearning means being indistinguishable from it.

**TOFU** (Task of Fictitious Unlearning, Maini et al., 2024) makes that reference cheap. It contains 200 fictitious author profiles with 20 question-answer pairs each, generated with GPT-4 so no pretrained model knows them. You fine-tune a model on all of them, then unlearn a forget split of 1%, 5% or 10% of the authors. Because the facts are invented, a **retain model** fine-tuned only on the other authors is a true never-saw-it reference.

The key per-question quantity is the **truth ratio**. Using length-normalized probabilities $P(a \mid q)^{1/|a|}$, compare a GPT-4 paraphrase $\tilde a$ of the correct answer with five perturbed, factually wrong answers $\hat a$ in the same template. Paraphrasing matters because the model was fine-tuned on one exact phrasing, which inflates its probability.

blocks.tex: R_{\text{truth}} = \frac{\frac{1}{|A_{\text{pert}}|}\sum_{\hat a \in A_{\text{pert}}} P(\hat a \mid q)^{1/|\hat a|}}{P(\tilde a \mid q)^{1/|\tilde a|}}
blocks.caption: Small R means the model strongly prefers the true answer. R near 1 means it cannot tell true from false.

blocks.md: A worked example with assumed normalized probabilities: the paraphrased true answer gets 0.40 and the five wrong answers get 0.10, 0.08, 0.12, 0.06, 0.09 (mean 0.09). Then $R = 0.09 / 0.40 = 0.225$: the model knows the fact. If unlearning lowers the true answer to 0.09 with the wrong ones unchanged, $R = 1.0$: no preference left.

**Forget quality** is a statistical test, not an average. Compute truth ratios on every forget-set question for both the unlearned model and the retain model, then run a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on the two distributions. The p-value is the forget quality: high means you cannot tell the two models apart, low means the unlearned model is still distinguishable. **Model utility** is the harmonic mean of nine numbers: probability, ROUGE and truth ratio on the retain set, on real authors, and on world facts.

blocks.title: TOFU model utility: why a harmonic mean

scenes.caption: Model utility combines 3 metrics (probability, ROUGE, truth ratio) on 3 datasets (retain set, real authors, world facts). Made-up but typical values: arithmetic mean 0.809, harmonic mean 0.804.
Now one ability collapses to 0.02. The arithmetic mean only drops to 0.724, hiding the failure. The harmonic mean falls to 0.150, so the model is flagged as broken.

blocks.md: TOFU's baseline result was sobering. In the paper's Phi-1.5 runs with the 1% forget split (Llama-2-7B showed the same trends), gradient ascent, gradient difference, KL minimization and an "I don't know" preference baseline all failed to reach meaningful forget quality (every p-value below 0.001), and forgetting more than 1% caused severe utility drops. NPO, from Lesson 2, was later the first to reach forget quality above 0.05 on much larger splits.

**MUSE** (Shi et al., 2024) widens the view to six criteria, three for data owners and three for deployers:

1. no verbatim memorization (VerbMem),
2. no knowledge memorization (KnowMem, QA about the forget set),
3. no privacy leakage (PrivLeak, from a membership inference attack),
4. utility preserved on the retain set,
5. scalability to large forget sets,
6. sustainability over sequential requests.

It uses two corpora: BBC news articles and the Harry Potter books, with 7B models.

scenes.caption: KnowMem on the forget set (lower means less knowledge revealed). The retrained model still scores 33.1, not 0: some forget-set answers follow from general knowledge.

KnowMem on the retain set (utility, higher is better). GA reaches 0 forgetting by reaching 0 utility. Every method loses utility relative to the retrained model's 55.0 except Task Vector, which also forgot nothing.

blocks.md: **PrivLeak** compares how well a membership inference attack (Min-K% Prob) separates forget data from held-out data, normalized by the same AUC for the retrained model; it should be near 0. Large positive values mean **over-unlearning** (the forget set now looks *less* familiar than unseen data, which itself leaks membership) and large negative values mean **under-unlearning**. On NEWS, gradient difference variants scored above +100% and KL-regularized variants about -96%; the paper reports that only one of eight methods avoided severe leakage, and that most degraded utility, scaled poorly to larger forget sets, and degraded over sequential requests.

blocks.prompt: On MUSE NEWS, plain GA and plain NPO both score exactly 0 on VerbMem and KnowMem for the forget set, better than the retrained model's 20.8 and 33.1. Are they the best unlearning methods in the table?
blocks.reveal: No. Both also score 0 on retain-set KnowMem: the models are unusable. And scoring *below* the retrained model on the forget set is itself a signal, since a never-trained model would still answer about a third of those questions from general knowledge. The target is to match the retrained model, not to minimize forget metrics.

blocks.md: Unlearning is judged against the retrained model on two axes at once: forget metrics should match it (not undershoot it) and utility should stay near it. Under-unlearning and over-unlearning both leak that the data was there.

blocks.question: Your unlearned model gets a TOFU forget quality (KS-test p-value) of 0.0004. What does that mean?
options: The model forgot 99.96% of the forget set
The model's utility is 0.0004
The model is statistically indistinguishable from the retain model
The truth-ratio distribution on the forget set is very unlikely to come from the same distribution as the retain model's, so unlearning is incomplete or overshot
blocks.explain: Forget quality is the p-value of a two-sample KS test between the unlearned and retain models' truth-ratio distributions. A tiny p-value means the distributions clearly differ, which is poor unlearning in either direction. It is not a percentage of facts forgotten.

blocks.question: Why does TOFU aggregate its nine utility numbers with a harmonic mean rather than an arithmetic mean?
options: It is faster to compute
So that one collapsed ability drags the score down instead of being averaged away
Because the metrics have different units
So that utility is always at least 0.5
blocks.explain: A harmonic mean is dominated by its smallest inputs. In the example, one score dropping to 0.02 moves the arithmetic mean only to 0.724 but the harmonic mean to 0.150. The TOFU authors chose it for exactly this reason: they did not want low scores to be averaged out.

lessons.title: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks

blocks.md: Every method so far changes what the model *says*. The adversarial question is whether the knowledge is still recoverable from the weights. Lynch et al. (2024) ran eight such tests on the Who's Harry Potter model: prompts in other languages, jailbreak prompts, in-context relearning, relearning by fine-tuning, downstream question answering, latent knowledge probes, comparison with a trivial prompting baseline, and side effects on related domains.

blocks.title: Relearning: a little data brings the knowledge back

scenes.caption: The provider runs unlearning and releases the weights. Standard evaluations look good.
Asked directly, the model gives a generic or wrong answer.
With open weights, the attacker fine-tunes on a small, possibly loosely related dataset. Lynch et al. used 800 or 8,000 sentences (about 1% or 10% of the books); Hu et al. used public, benign text.
The suppressed knowledge resurfaces, including facts that were not in the relearning data. Hu et al. recovered bioweapons-related knowledge by relearning on public medical articles.

blocks.md: Relearning attacks are cheap. Lynch et al. found fine-tuning on 8,000 sentences brought the WHP model close to the original's performance. The WMDP authors fine-tuned an RMU-unlearned Mistral-7B on the cybersecurity forget corpus and found RMU was unable to prevent recovery. Hu et al. (2024) showed that even *benign*, loosely related data works: general wiki text about the series brought back verbatim memorized passages. They conclude that current approximate methods suppress outputs rather than remove knowledge.

Quantization is an even cheaper attack because users do it routinely to run models on smaller GPUs. Zhang et al. (2024) quantized unlearned models from the MUSE benchmark. For unlearning methods with utility constraints, the full-precision models retained on average 21% of the knowledge meant to be forgotten; after 4-bit quantization they retained 83%. 8-bit models behaved like full precision. Different 4-bit methods (round-to-nearest, GPTQ, AWQ) gave similar results.

blocks.caption: Round-to-nearest with N bits as written in the paper. Every weight within half a step of a grid point maps to the same integer, so updates smaller than Delta / 2 are invisible.

blocks.title: Why 4-bit rounding erases a small unlearning update

scenes.caption: Six weights of one tensor before and after unlearning. Utility-preserving unlearning uses small learning rates, so each weight moved by at most 0.006. Max |w| = 0.8.

Int-4 round-to-nearest: step = 0.8 / 2^3 = 0.1, so any change smaller than half a step (0.05) can vanish. All six unlearned weights round to the same integer as the originals: the quantized unlearned model IS the quantized original.
Int-8: step = 0.8 / 2^7 = 0.00625, half a step 0.003125. Now 3 of the 6 weights land in a different bin, so part of the unlearning survives quantization.

blocks.md: The paper explains this exactly as the figure does: utility-preserving unlearning uses small learning rates (MUSE and TOFU use peak rates of 1e-5 or below, versus 1e-4 to 3e-4 for pretraining models such as GPT-3 and Llama 3), so most weights move less than half a 4-bit step and $Q(f_{\text{unlearn}}) \approx Q(f_{\text{target}})$. The one apparent exception, plain GA, only survived quantization because it had already destroyed the model's utility.

A model that passes forget-set benchmarks in full precision can fail them after an ordinary 4-bit conversion that a user applies for deployment. Any release that relies on unlearning should evaluate the quantized versions people will actually run.

What to do in practice:

- If you need a guarantee (legal deletion), only exact methods give one: retrain without the data, or design training for it (SISA-style sharding, or periodic retraining from filtered data).
- Treat approximate unlearning of open-weight models as output suppression that a motivated attacker can undo. The WMDP authors scope RMU to a closed-model threat model where the provider applies unlearning before serving.
- Evaluate adversarially: paraphrases and other languages, jailbreaks, in-context hints, few-step fine-tuning on related data, probes on hidden states, and quantization, always against a retrained reference.

Low scores on forget benchmarks show suppressed outputs, not erased knowledge. Small fine-tunes, probes and even 4-bit quantization can bring "forgotten" knowledge back, because approximate unlearning moves the weights only slightly.

blocks.question: Unlearned model A uses a small learning rate plus a retain loss and keeps 95% of its utility. Model B used plain gradient ascent and collapsed to near-zero utility. After 4-bit quantization, which is more likely to reveal the forgotten knowledge again?
options: A, because its small weight changes mostly fall inside the same quantization bins as the original weights
B, because gradient ascent changes few weights
Neither, quantization only reduces precision and cannot restore information
Both equally, quantization resets every model to the original
blocks.explain: Quantization maps every weight within half a step of a grid point to the same value. Utility-preserving unlearning moves weights by tiny amounts, so the quantized unlearned model is nearly the quantized original, which still knows the facts. Zhang et al. saw 21% retained knowledge rise to 83% at 4 bits; GA was the exception only because it had wrecked the model.

blocks.question: A lab applies RMU to an open-weight model and publishes near-chance WMDP scores as evidence the model is safe to release. What is the strongest objection?
options: WMDP has too few questions to be meaningful
RMU always destroys general capabilities
With open weights anyone can fine-tune on related data, and RMU did not prevent relearning in the WMDP paper's own fine-tuning experiment
Near-chance scores prove the model was never trained on the data
blocks.explain: The WMDP appendix reports that fine-tuning an RMU-unlearned Mistral-7B on the forget corpus recovered performance, and Hu et al. show even benign related data can jog the knowledge back. RMU's stated threat model is a closed model unlearned just before serving, not a public release.
